title: Non-melanoma skin cancer
intro: Basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma are the most common cancers worldwide. They usually develop on sun-exposed skin and grow slowly. They are generally curable when treated early, and rarely spread, although squamous cell cancer is more likely than basal cell cancer to do so.

sections.heading: Causes and risk
paragraphs: Long-term exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun and sunbeds is the main cause. Risk is higher with fair skin, older age, sunburn history, weakened immunity such as after organ transplant, and previous skin cancer. Rough, scaly patches called actinic keratoses can progress to squamous cell cancer.

sections.heading: What it looks like
paragraphs: Basal cell cancer often looks like a pearly or waxy bump, a flat scar-like patch or a sore that bleeds and does not heal. Squamous cell cancer appears as a scaly red patch, firm lump or crusted ulcer. Any new spot that grows, bleeds or does not heal within a month or two should be examined.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and treatment
paragraphs: A doctor examines the skin and usually removes the lesion or a small sample for examination under the microscope. Most tumours are removed surgically with a margin of healthy skin. Superficial tumours may be treated by scraping, freezing, creams, photodynamic therapy or radiotherapy. Specialised micrographic surgery is used for high-risk areas such as the face.

sections.heading: Follow-up and prevention
paragraphs: Having one skin cancer raises the risk of others, so regular skin checks are advised. Protect skin from the sun with shade, clothing, hats and sunscreen, avoid sunbeds and examine your skin regularly.

sections.heading: Living with a history of skin cancer
paragraphs: Many people feel anxious after a diagnosis. Learning what to look for, keeping appointments and protecting your skin gives a sense of control. Tell relatives, because family members may share risk factors such as fair skin.

examples.title: Noticing a spot
examples.text: Imagine you have a sore on your nose that bleeds and does not heal. You could book a skin check promptly and bring a photo showing when you first noticed it.

examples.title: Planning protection
examples.text: Suppose you work outdoors. You might wear a wide-brimmed hat and long sleeves, apply sunscreen to exposed skin and have an annual skin check.
